title: How to Build a Safer Public Contact Form
content:
A public contact form accepts messages from people you do not know, then moves those messages into systems your team trusts. That transition is the security problem. A safe design limits what can arrive, controls where it goes, preserves a usable experience, and prevents a successful submission from becoming a path into email, storage, or an administrative interface.

Keep the input contract narrow

Begin with the actual purpose: receive a message and a reply address. Avoid collecting telephone numbers, company profiles, location, or attachments unless the workflow requires them. Define allowed fields, types, lengths, and request size on the server. Browser validation improves usability, but an attacker can send a request without using your form.

The OWASP input-validation guidance distinguishes validation of structure and meaning and favors allowlisted expectations where appropriate. For a contact form, an email field has a different contract from a free-text message. Do not use a narrow alphabet-only rule for names or prose; legitimate Unicode text and punctuation need to remain usable.

Reject unexpected structures, such as an array where a string is expected, and bound processing before expensive work begins. Keep user-facing errors specific enough to repair the input without revealing internal implementation details. Validation is one layer: it does not replace parameterized storage operations or context-appropriate output encoding when the message is displayed.

Separate message content from delivery controls

Choose the recipient on the server from approved configuration. Do not let an arbitrary browser field select the destination mailbox, SMTP host, or sender account. Use the organization's authenticated sending identity and place a validated reply address in the appropriate reply field. Treat newline characters and other header-sensitive content carefully through a maintained email library.

Do not render submitted HTML directly in the staff interface. A plain-text message is often sufficient. If rich text is a genuine requirement, sanitize it with a maintained library under a restrictive policy and encode content for its output context. A message that appears harmless in a confirmation email can behave differently in an HTML dashboard or exported spreadsheet.

Choose abuse controls without excluding people

Apply limits around submission frequency, payload size, and expensive downstream operations. Consider shared networks when choosing identifiers. A hidden field or challenge can supplement controls but should not be the sole defense. Evaluate accessibility and failure recovery before deploying a challenge that legitimate visitors cannot complete. Keep the message available when a temporary error occurs.

CSRF protection depends on the endpoint's context. The OWASP CSRF guidance describes defenses for unwanted browser-originated state-changing requests, particularly where credentials are automatically attached. A public unauthenticated form has different concerns from a signed-in support action. Use framework protections where applicable, and do not treat CORS configuration as a universal anti-spam or CSRF solution.

Respond consistently whether or not a submitted email belongs to an existing account. Otherwise a contact endpoint may disclose membership information. Keep success claims narrow: “message received” should correspond to durable acceptance, not merely a button click. If delivery is queued, distinguish accepted from actually delivered so staff and visitors are not misled during a provider outage.

A hypothetical small-business form

Imagine a hypothetical studio that needs a name, reply email, and project message. Its first implementation sends the entire request object to a mailbox selected by a browser parameter. The revised design accepts only three fields, chooses the destination from server configuration, and queues a plain-text message with an internal request identifier. Attachments are omitted because the initial consultation does not require them.

The test set includes a normal Unicode name, an overly long message, duplicate submission, an unexpected object value, and a message containing HTML-like text. Staff see that text as text rather than executable content. The team checks provider failure separately: accepted queued messages remain visible to staff, while an unavailable queue produces an honest retry message rather than an unconditional success screen.

This example is hypothetical and does not establish that a specific form is secure. Its review also covers keyboard navigation, field labels, focus after validation failure, and whether errors preserve the visitor's message. A perfectly enforced input length is not enough if people lose a carefully written inquiry every time connectivity drops.

Limit retention and protect operational access

Store messages only where the team has a reason and a reviewed retention policy. Avoid copying the full body into application logs, analytics, and exception reports. Use request identifiers and outcome codes for routine diagnostics. Restrict access to inboxes and administrative views, and ensure that deleting a message does not leave an unrestricted public attachment or forgotten export.

If files become necessary later, treat that as a new feature with separate type, size, storage, scanning, download-authorization, and retention decisions. Renaming an uploaded file does not make it safe. Keep credentials in server-side secret storage and never include them in the static page bundle. Browser code is delivered to visitors, regardless of whether the source is minified.

Document who investigates failed delivery, how to pause the form during abuse, and which alternative contact route is available. Test these operations with synthetic messages. Do not send bulk test traffic to an unrelated production mailbox or assume a provider's accepted response proves that a human received the email.

Contact-form checklist

  • Minimize fields and enforce a server-side schema and size budget.
  • Keep recipients, sender identity, and delivery credentials server-controlled.
  • Render messages safely in every staff and export destination.
  • Use context-appropriate CSRF and abuse controls.
  • Preserve input and provide accessible, accurate feedback.
  • Distinguish queued acceptance from actual delivery.
  • Document retention, delivery failure, and a safe pause procedure.
excerpt: Build a safer public contact form with narrow server validation, fixed delivery controls, safe staff rendering, accessible errors, and honest queued-message feedback.
